instructions.name: bid
docs: Phase 1. Irrevocable deposit. There is no withdraw instruction, by design.

accounts.name: commitment
docs: Accumulates across repeat bids from the same wallet. Splitting a bid across many
wallets and concentrating it in one are worth exactly the same — that is the
point of pro-rata, and it is why no per-wallet cap exists here.

accounts.name: jito_dont_front
docs: entire mechanism; see `JITO_DONT_FRONT`.

instructions.name: burn_unsold
docs: Phase 4. Permissionless. Burns the supply nobody bought, which is otherwise locked
in the vault forever.

accounts.name: payer
docs: Anyone. Pays the fee and receives nothing.

instructions.name: claim
docs: Phase 3. Tokens plus any pro-rata excess, on a Succeeded sale. Bidder signs.

instructions.name: fail_on_missing_pool
docs: Permissionless recovery: no pool by `pool_deadline` means every claim refunds.

instructions.name: finalize
docs: Phase 2. Permissionless. Freezes `total_committed` and settles against the floor.

instructions.name: initialize_sale
docs: Phase 0. Verifies the vault is safe, records the terms, opens bidding.

accounts.name: token_vault
docs: The tokens being sold. Funded *before* this instruction runs; this instruction's
job is to verify it, not to trust it.

accounts.name: sol_vault
docs: The single shared SOL vault: a system-owned PDA. Never created here — bidders'
transfers fund it, and the program signs with these seeds to move SOL out.
Seeded to rent-exempt minimum below so it cannot be reaped.

accounts.name: seed_destination
docs: Where proceeds may go, and nowhere else. Recorded now so it is publicly readable
before the first bid.

instructions.name: mark_pool_created
docs: Permissionless. Proves the pool exists and its LP is burned; unblocks claims.

accounts.name: lp_mint
docs: The pool's LP mint. Its `supply` is the only trustworthy evidence of a burn.

instructions.name: refund
docs: Phase 3, the recovery half. Full principal on a Failed sale. **Permissionless**,
and deliberately free of the allocation math — see the module docs on `claim.rs`.

accounts.name: payer
docs: Anyone. Pays the fee and receives nothing.

accounts.name: bidder
docs: again in the handler. Receives the lamports; never signs.

accounts.name: sale
docs: Not `mut`. `refund` never writes the sale account, so refunds do not queue behind
one write lock and a bug in the claim bookkeeping cannot reach principal.

instructions.name: sweep_proceeds
docs: Phase 4. Permissionless. Moves the raise to the pre-committed `seed_destination`.
**Gated on `pool_created`** — without that gate it destroys bidder principal.

accounts.name: payer
docs: Anyone. Pays the fee and receives nothing.

accounts.name: seed_destination
docs: verified about it, and nothing else needs to be — it was published in advance.

types.name: Commitment
docs: One per bidder, at ["commit", sale, bidder]. Every per-bidder decision lives here, so a
claimer needs only this account, the frozen totals, and a constant — no merkle root and
no settlement authority that could strand principal.
`refund` writes only this account and the SOL vault; it never touches `Sale`. That keeps
the principal-recovery path independent of the allocation bookkeeping, and it lets
refunds run in parallel instead of queueing on one write lock.

fields.name: amount
docs: Total lamports committed. Accumulates across repeat bids. Irrevocable.

fields.name: tokens_claimed
docs: Tokens received. Set once.

fields.name: lamports_refunded
docs: Lamports refunded (excess above the cap, or the full amount if Failed). Set once.

types.name: Sale
docs: One per token mint. Written at initialize, frozen in shape thereafter.
Everything a claimer needs is here plus their own `Commitment`: pro-rata is a fold, so
there is no merkle root and no settlement authority that could strand principal.

fields.name: authority
docs: Funds the sale and seeds the pool afterwards. Holds no power over bidder principal.

fields.name: token_mint
docs: The token being sold.

fields.name: token_vault
docs: Program-owned token account holding the tokens. Verified in Phase 0.

fields.name: sol_vault
docs: The single shared SOL vault PDA.

fields.name: seed_destination
docs: Where proceeds may go, and nowhere else. Pre-committed and publicly readable
before anyone bids — this is the account that makes "the builder cannot redirect
your SOL" checkable rather than promised.

fields.name: price_lamports
docs: Lamports per whole token (per 10^decimals base units).

fields.name: supply_for_sale
docs: Base units of the token available. Never exceeds the vault's spendable balance.

fields.name: hard_cap_lamports
docs: Lamports. Commitments above this are refunded pro-rata.

fields.name: floor_lamports
docs: Lamports. Below this at close the sale Fails and everyone refunds in full.

fields.name: min_bid_lamports
docs: Lamports. Dust-griefing deterrent; the real cost to an attacker is the lockup.

fields.name: total_committed
docs: Frozen at finalize. Until then it only grows.

fields.name: total_claimed_tokens
docs: Bookkeeping for the invariant `sum(alloc) <= supply_for_sale`.

fields.name: total_accepted_lamports
docs: Lamports actually kept from settled commitments — the sum of `accepted_i`, which is
what `sweep_proceeds` is allowed to move.
**Not `hard_cap_lamports`, and the difference is not zero.** Oversubscribed,
`accepted_i = floor(c_i * cap / C)` and flooring loses up to one lamport per bidder,
so `sum(accepted_i)` lands *below* the cap by up to N-1 lamports. Sweeping the cap
instead would leave the last refunder's transaction short — the same failure mode as
over-allocating tokens, transposed onto principal. Recorded here at settle time so a
sweep never has to infer it. It is also why `sweep_proceeds` must run after claims,
or move only what has been recorded so far.

fields.name: claim_count
docs: How many bidders have claimed tokens. Deliberately not incremented by `refund`,
which does not write this account at all.
Load-bearing in exactly one place: `burn_unsold` requires
`claim_count == commitment_count`, because until then the unsold remainder is not
distinguishable from tokens someone is still owed.

fields.name: commitment_count
docs: Distinct `Commitment` accounts ever created, incremented by `bid` on first creation.
Two uses, both of which need a count rather than a sum:
1. `sweep_proceeds` before claims settle. Oversubscribed, the sale retains
`sum(floor(c_i * cap / C))`, which is not computable without iterating every
commitment — but flooring loses under one lamport each, so it is strictly greater
than `cap - commitment_count`. That bound is safe at any time, including before
the first claim, which is when the sweep actually has to run.
2. `burn_unsold`, as the definition of "everyone has claimed".

fields.name: close_ts
docs: Extends on late activity, capped by `MAX_EXTENSIONS` and `absolute_deadline`.

fields.name: absolute_deadline
docs: `close_ts` can never pass this, however much late activity there is.

fields.name: pool_deadline
docs: If the pool does not exist by here, claims flip permissionlessly to full refund.
This is what turns "the builder disappeared" into self-executing recovery.

fields.name: pool_created
docs: Set once the pool has been created and seeded.
**INVARIANT — both halves required, and `claim` owns the second one:**
1. `fail_on_missing_pool` may flip a sale to `Failed` only while `!pool_created`.
2. `claim` MUST `require!(sale.pool_created)`.
Together these make the two states mutually exclusive, so a sale can never flip to
`Failed` after someone has already claimed tokens. Drop half 2 and the abandonment
path becomes a way for early claimers to keep tokens while everyone else refunds.
It also matches the launch sequence, where claims open only after trading is live.

fields.name: total_swept_lamports
docs: Lamports already moved to `seed_destination`. A running total, not a flag, because
the sweep is re-callable: the amount it may safely move grows as claims settle.

fields.name: unsold_burned
docs: Set once the unsold remainder has been burned. One shot — the burnable amount is a
function of state that does not change afterwards, so a flag is the only guard.

fields.name: pool
docs: The verified Raydium CPMM pool. Default until `mark_pool_created` proves one.

fields.name: pool_open_time
docs: The pool's `open_time`, copied from pool state once verified.
**`claim` MUST require `now >= pool_open_time`.** Claims opening only after trading
is live is what makes the opening price safe: at the moment the pool goes live the
circulating float is zero, so nobody holds tokens to dump into an overpriced pool.
Reverse the order and opening high builds a sell-side snipe instead of preventing a
buy-side one. Enforcing it here makes that ordering a program rule rather than a
procedure someone has to follow correctly on launch day.

types.name: SaleParams
docs: Everything the sale needs, decided before anyone may bid.
The four numbers (price, cap, floor, window) are parameters, not constants — they are
still undecided at the time of writing and do not block the mechanism.

constants.name: COMMIT_SEED
docs: PDA seed for a bidder's `Commitment`: ["commit", sale, bidder].

constants.name: EXTENSION_SECONDS
docs: How far past `close_ts` a qualifying late bid pushes the close, in seconds.

constants.name: EXTENSION_TRIGGER_SECONDS
docs: A bid landing within this window before `close_ts` triggers an extension.

constants.name: JITO_DONT_FRONT
docs: Jito's anti-sandwich marker.
Any pubkey whose base58 begins with `jitodontfront`, present in any instruction, makes
the Jito block engine reject a bundle unless this transaction sits at index 0. Padding
the prefix with `1`s yields exactly one valid 32-byte key, which is this one.
**Honest scope:** this is anti-sandwich only, enforced off-chain by one block engine.
Transactions submitted directly to validators are not covered, and it prevents nothing
about bid ordering — which is worth zero here anyway, by design.

constants.name: MAX_EXTENSIONS
docs: Hard ceiling on how many times late activity may push `close_ts` out.
Without a cap an attacker controls the deadline indefinitely at minimum-bid cost.
The absolute deadline sits behind this as a second backstop.

constants.name: RAYDIUM_CPMM_PROGRAM
docs: Owner of a genuine CPMM pool account.
**Both values are confirmed against live pools, not documentation.** A wrong program
id here is the easiest possible way to accept a counterfeit pool.
- devnet: the `owner` of our own pool `6zKJcfz…`, read 2026-08-08
- mainnet: the `owner` of live pool `H1Kvn7XW1qh9BP9kKo2KZqz8Q6ZcppsJCsUDxJEvntav`,
read 2026-08-08 with `tools/verify-mainnet-cpmm.py`. That pool is 637 bytes with the
same discriminator, so the layout below holds on mainnet too.

constants.name: SALE_SEED
docs: PDA seed for the one `Sale` account per token mint.

constants.name: SOL_VAULT_SEED
docs: PDA seed for the single shared SOL vault: ["sol_vault", sale].
One shared vault, not one per bidder. Per-bidder custody and decoupled refunds are
mutually exclusive, and per-bidder accounts would make pool seeding an N-account sweep.
